To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in vitro the uptake of liposomes by endothelial and kupffer cells is inhibited in a similar way by poly (I) and other anion macromolecules, whereas in vivo the liposome uptake by hepatocytes and kupffer cells but not by endothelial cells is inhibited by serum.

the uptake of phosphatidylethanolamine-containing liposomes is mainly determined by the presence of phosphatidic acid in the membrane, whereas the uptake of phospholipids containing phosphatidicserine is mainly determined by its amount in the membrane.
the uptake of phosphatidylester liposomes by sinusoidal endothelial and Kupffers cells is inhibited by plasma proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the uptake of liposomes by the liver in vivo and in primary culture, with a special emphasis on the uptake by endothelial, Kupffer, and parenchymal liver cells.
a new concept for the interaction between liposomes and the liver.
the in vitro-in vivo differences of the interaction of phosphatidylethanolamine-containing liposomes with sinusoidal liver cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
liposomes containing phospholipids with negatively charged head groups, which are able to be internalized by liver cells, are only taken up to a limited extent in vivo.
the uptake of phosphatidylethanolamine-containing liposomes by sinusoidal cells in vivo and in primary culture is different.
the in vivo and in vivo/in vitro differences in liposomal uptake by liver cells are due to the presence of plasma proteins, which mask phosphatidyl serine head groups.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the liver cells, in vivo and in primary culture, recognize the phosphatidyserine head groups of liposomes by the same receptor, but in vivo the liposomes are protected from this recognition by plasma proteins.
liposome uptake by liver cells in vitro is not representative for the uptake by the liver in vivo.
the in vivo and in vivo-in vitro results are not contradictory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
liposome uptake by liver cells is not only a matter of liposomal surface characteristics but is also influenced by the presence of plasma proteins.
liposomal phosphatidyserine is recognized by the liver in vivo but is not recognized by endothelial cells in vivo.
the in vitro uptake of phosphatidylethanolamine-containing liposomes is a useful model for studying the in vivo uptake of these liposomes.
